sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) with glomerulonephritis (AAV-GN) is classically considered pauci-immune, yet complement activation is a central pathogenic mechanism. Whether intrarenal complement-related transcriptional programs are reflected by conventional serum or immunofluorescence markers, and whether they are clinically informative, remains unclear.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In 369 patients with AAV-GN from 2 independent retrospective cohorts, complement was assessed across circulating, histopathologic, and transcriptomic layers (serum C3/C4, glomerular C1q/C3 deposition, and targeted kidney transcriptomics). Predefined classical and alternative pathway-related expression scores were derived from intrarenal gene expression. Associations with severity and outcomes were evaluated using multivariable Cox models. Public spatial transcriptomic data sets provided validation and localization.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Below-normal serum C3/C4 levels were uncommon. Low serum C3, but not C4, was associated with more severe kidney involvement, kidney failure (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]: 2.0 [1.1–3.7]), and mortality (aHR: 2.3 [1.3–4.0]). Both glomerular C3 (47%) and C1q (11%) deposition identified more severe pathology and adverse outcomes. Compared with controls, AAV-GN kidneys showed increased complement-related expression—including classical pathway components, proximal alternative pathway genes (C3, C5AR1), and regulatory transcripts—that was only weakly concordant with serum or deposition markers. Low alternative pathway-related expression was independently associated with better kidney (aHR: 0.3 [0.1–0.7]) and overall (aHR: 0.4 [0.2–0.9]) survival. Spatial transcriptomics validated these signatures and suggested contributions from both immune and resident kidney compartments.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: AAV-GN displays a reproducible intrarenal complement-related transcriptional program, only weakly captured by serum levels or routine immunofluorescence, associated with renal severity and outcomes. These findings support prospective studies integrating tissue complement transcriptomics for stratification and therapeutic hypothesis generation.

body.p: AAV are necrotizing small-vessel vasculitides in which renal involvement, manifesting as crescentic glomerulonephritis (AAV-GN), is a major determinant of long-term prognosis.1 Despite advances in immunosuppressive strategies, a substantial proportion of patients progress to kidney failure or relapse, highlighting the need for improved risk stratification and a deeper understanding of intrarenal disease mechanisms.2 Over the past 2 decades, the complement system has emerged as a key amplifier of ANCA-mediated inflammation,3 with a central role for the alternative pathway and the C5a-C5aR axis.4

However, the contribution of complement in human AAV-GN remains incompletely characterized. In clinical practice and observational studies, complement involvement is most often assessed using circulating C3/C4 levels and glomerular C1q/C3 deposition by immunofluorescence. Although AAV-GN is classically described as pauci-immune, low or low-normal serum C3 levels have been associated with more severe renal disease and poorer outcomes,5,6 and glomerular complement deposition is frequently detected in kidneys.7, 8, 9 Proteomic studies have further shown that complement proteins may be present within glomeruli even when routine immunofluorescence is negative.10 These observations indicate that serum levels, immunofluorescence deposits, protein-level complement detection, and intrarenal complement-related gene expression represent distinct biological layers whose relationships and clinical relevance remain poorly defined.

Targeted bulk transcriptomics from diagnostic biopsies have identified complement-related genes as major correlates of kidney function and prognosis in AAV-GN,11 whereas spatial transcriptomics now enables compartment- and cell-type–resolved profiling of kidney tissue. Earlier intrarenal complement gene-expression work in AAV-GN12 further supports the relevance of tissue-level complement profiling in this setting. Whether intrarenal complement-related transcriptional programs are concordant with conventional serum and immunofluorescence markers, and whether they carry clinical information beyond these markers, remains unknown.

Here, we evaluated predefined intrarenal complement pathway-related expression scores in AAV-GN, their association with kidney severity and clinical outcomes, and their concordance with circulating C3/C4 levels and glomerular C1q/C3 deposition. We then leveraged publicly available spatial transcriptomic data sets to validate these bulk transcriptomic signatures, define their compartmental and cell-type distribution, and assess their cross-platform reproducibility.

sec.title: Selection of Patients and Controls
sec.p: As previously described,11,13 2 independent cohorts of patients with AAV-GN were included in this study—the Maine-Anjou registry14,15 and the RENVAS registry16,17 (Figure 1a). Control kidney samples (n = 23) were included for transcriptomic comparisons (Supplementary Table S1). Detailed methods regarding patient selection, clinical data collection, outcome definitions, pathologic assessment, and ethical considerations are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

sec.title: Complement Assessment in the Main Cohort
sec.p: Complement was assessed across 3 complementary layers—circulating complement levels, glomerular complement deposition, and intrarenal complement-related gene expression. Serum C3 and C4 levels were measured as part of routine clinical care before remission-induction immunosuppressive therapy. Glomerular C1q and C3 deposition were assessed by routine indirect immunofluorescence on initial diagnostic kidney biopsy and analyzed as absent versus detectable deposition. Intrarenal gene expression was assessed using targeted bulk NanoString transcriptomics using the same formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded initial diagnostic kidney biopsy specimens, as previously reported.11,13 The present study used the curated, normalized expression matrix for complement-focused analyses (Supplementary Methods). Predefined complement pathway–related expression scores were generated from the following selected genes: C1QA, C1QB, C2, and C4A.B for the classical pathway, and C3, CFB, CFP, and CFD for the alternative pathway. For each sample, gene-wise z scores were averaged to derive classical and alternative pathway expression scores, referred to as cCP_path and cAP_path, respectively. Throughout the manuscript, “pathway score” refers to these predefined transcriptomic expression scores and not to a direct biochemical measurement of complement pathway activity. C5, C5AR1, and complement regulatory genes, including CFH, CD46, CD55, and CD59, were analyzed separately.

sec.title: External Spatial Transcriptomic Data Sets
sec.p: Publicly available spatial transcriptomic data sets were used to validate the complement-related transcriptional signatures identified above and to localize these signatures beyond bulk tissue expression (Figure 1a). Sequencing-based spatial transcriptomic data from Engesser et al.18 were used to assess complement-related expression across spatially annotated kidney compartments. Imaging-based spatial transcriptomic data from Sultana et al.19 were used to evaluate complement-related expression at cell-type resolution.

For both data sets, original compartment or cell-type annotations provided by the source studies were used without de novo reannotation. Complement pathway-related scores and individual gene-expression values were aggregated using patient-, compartment-, or cell-type-level pseudobulk approaches, as appropriate. Detailed processing steps are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables were described as median (first–third quartiles), and categorical variables as counts and percentages. Group comparisons for transcriptomic data were performed using t test on log2-transformed or normalized expression values, as appropriate, and effect sizes were reported as Cohen d. Correlations were assessed using Spearman correlation coefficient.

Survival analyses were performed using Kaplan–Meier curves, log-rank tests, and Cox proportional hazards models. Outcomes included kidney failure, kidney-involving relapse, and all-cause mortality. Multivariable Cox models were adjusted for age, sex, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at diagnosis, and AAV phenotype. Because the objective was to evaluate associations with each outcome rather than estimate cumulative incidence in the presence of competing events, kidney failure and relapse models were interpreted as cause-specific association models; death was analyzed as a separate end point. Restricted cubic spline Cox models were used as sensitivity analyses to assess potential nonlinear associations between continuous complement markers and outcomes. Results are reported as HRs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate procedure within predefined analytical families, except for Cox survival models, which were reported using nominal P values. Missing data were not imputed. Analyses were performed using available-case data for each complement modality and complete-case data for multivariable models. Statistical analyses were performed using R v4.0. Additional statistical methods are described in the Supplementary Methods.

sec.title: Study Population, Outcomes, and Complement Assessment Modalities
sec.p: A total of 369 patients with AAV-GN were included. Baseline characteristics, treatments, and outcomes are detailed in Supplementary Table S2. Briefly, 60% of patients were male, with a predominance of microscopic polyangiitis (69%) and antimyeloperoxidase positivity (64%). Median age at diagnosis was 68 (57–74) years, median eGFR was 18 (11–37) ml/min, and median proteinuria was 1.4 (0.8–2.7) g/g. Histologically, Berden classes20 were distributed as follows: focal (29%), crescentic (35%), mixed (23%), and sclerotic (13%). Median interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy was 20%, and interstitial inflammation was graded as i1 in 54%, i2 in 28%, and i3 in 19% of patients. After a median follow-up of 60 (28–110) months, 104 of 369 (29%) patients progressed to kidney failure, 61 (17%) experienced kidney-involving relapse, and 115 (31%) died (Figure 1b).

Complement was assessed across 3 modalities—serum C3 and/or C4 in 263 (71%) patients, glomerular immunofluorescence (C1q and/or C3) in 305 (83%) and 288 (78%), respectively, and kidney transcriptomics in 199 (54%). Most patients (273/369, 74%) had ≥ 2 modalities available, and 108 (29%) had all 3 (Figure 1c). Modality-specific subsets showed broadly similar baseline characteristics to the overall cohort (Supplementary Table S2).

sec.title: Conventional Complement Markers are Associated With Severity and Outcomes
sec.p: Below normal complement levels were rare (3.4% each, Figure 1d); therefore, it was analyzed using terciles. Serum C3 and C4 levels were moderately correlated (ρ = 0.47, q < 0.0001, Supplementary Figure S1B). Patients in the lowest C4 tercile were similar to those in the intermediate and high terciles, without differences in complement deposition or clinical outcomes after multivariable adjustment. In contrast, patients in the lowest C3 tercile were more likely to have myeloperoxidase-positive microscopic polyangiitis and had more severe kidney involvement at diagnosis, including lower eGFR and higher proteinuria. Low serum C3 was independently associated with kidney failure (aHR vs. intermediate tercile: 2.0 [1.1–3.7], P = 0.029) and death (aHR: 2.3 [1.3–4.0], P = 0.003), in models adjusted for age, sex, eGFR at diagnosis, and AAV phenotype (Table 1, Figure 2, Supplementary Figure S2). Restricted cubic spline analyses were consistent with higher risk at lower serum C3 values, particularly for mortality (Supplementary Figure S3).

sec.p: Detectable glomerular C1q deposition was present in 11% (35/305) of patients and C3 deposition in 47% (135/288) (Figure 1e). Both were associated with more severe renal pathology. Patients who were C1q-positive had higher proteinuria, fewer normal glomeruli, greater interstitial inflammation, and lower serum C3 levels. C1q deposition was independently associated with kidney failure (aHR: 2.2 [1.3–3.8], P = 0.043) and death (aHR: 2.6 [1.4–4.7], P = 0.002). Patients who were positive for C3 had lower eGFR, fewer normal glomeruli, more crescentic glomeruli, and lower serum C3 levels. C3 deposition was independently associated with increased mortality (aHR: 1.9 [1.2–3.1], P = 0.011), but not with kidney failure or relapse (Table 2, Figure 2, Supplementary Figure S2).

sec.title: Intrarenal Complement-Related Expression is Increased, Poorly Captured by Conventional Markers, and Clinically Relevant
Intrarenal Complement-Related Expression Programs are Increased and Linked to Inflammatory Cellular Signatures
sec.p: Compared with controls, AAV-GN kidneys displayed a marked complement-related transcriptional signature within the NanoString immune panel (Figure 3a, Supplementary Figure S1A). Several complement genes were upregulated, including classical pathway components C1QA, C1QB, and C2, the central complement component C3, C5AR1, proximal alternative pathway-related genes CFB and CFD, and the regulatory gene CFH. Accordingly, predefined classical and alternative pathway–related expression scores were higher in AAV-GN kidneys than in controls (q < 0.0001 for both; Figure 3b).

sec.p: These pathway-related expression scores correlated with kidney function, proteinuria, C-reactive protein, and histologic features (Figure 3c, Supplementary Figure S1B), but showed no meaningful correlation with Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (Table 3). In contrast, conventional complement markers showed little concordance with intrarenal complement-related transcriptional profiles. Serum C3 and C4 levels were not correlated with cCP_path or cAP_path expression scores, and only a limited gene-level association was observed between serum C4 and kidney C4A/B expression. Similarly, glomerular C1q or C3 deposition was not associated with intrarenal pathway-related expression scores or with a consistent kidney complement gene-expression pattern (Figure 3d, Supplementary Figure S1B and C, Table 3).

sec.p: Complement pathway-related expression scores were strongly correlated with NanoString-derived immune cell scores, particularly macrophage, neutrophil, dendritic-cell, and global leukocyte signatures (Figure 3e), indicating that bulk complement-related expression is closely linked to the inflammatory cellular architecture of AAV-GN lesions.

sec.title: Kidney Complement Pathway–Related Expression Scores Reflect Renal Severity and are Associated With Long-Term Outcomes
sec.p: Kidney complement-related genes showed strong intercorrelations (Supplementary Figure S1B). To capture pathway-level expression patterns, classical (cCP_path) and alternative (cAP_path) complement pathway-related expression scores were analyzed by terciles.

Patients with high kidney cCP_path score had more severe renal involvement at diagnosis, including lower eGFR, fewer normal glomeruli, and more frequent severe interstitial inflammation, compared with intermediate and low terciles. They also had higher C-reactive protein levels (Table 3). After multivariable adjustment, cCP_path was not independently associated with kidney failure, relapse, or death (Figure 2, Supplementary Figure S2).

High kidney cAP_path score was similarly associated with more severe renal disease at presentation, including lower eGFR, higher proteinuria, fewer normal glomeruli, and increased interstitial inflammation (Table 3). Low cAP_path expression was independently associated with lower kidney failure (aHR vs. intermediate tercile 0.3 [0.1–0.7], P = 0.007) and improved overall survival (aHR 0.4 [0.2–0.9], P = 0.03), in models adjusted for age, sex, eGFR at diagnosis, and AAV phenotype, whereas no association with kidney relapse was observed (Figure 2, Supplementary Figure S2). Restricted cubic spline analyses confirmed that the association between cAP_path and outcomes was not strictly monotonic and was mainly driven by a low-expression subgroup with favorable prognosis, without a clear graded increase in risk across higher cAP_path values (Supplementary Figure S3). Associations between individual complement gene expression and clinical outcomes are detailed in Supplementary Figure S4. Again, no association was found between cCP_path or cAP_path scores and serum C3/C4 levels or glomerular C1q/C3 deposition (Table 3).

Together, these findings indicate that intrarenal complement-related expression in AAV-GN is only partially reflected by circulating complement levels or glomerular deposition. The marked upregulation of complement-related transcripts therefore raises the question of their spatial origin within the renal parenchyma. We then used publicly available spatial transcriptomic data sets18,19 to assess the reproducibility of these transcriptional signatures and to localize their spatial and cellular distribution.

sec.title: Spatial Transcriptomics and Cross-Platform Meta-Analysis Support Reproducible Intrarenal Complement-Related Expression Signatures
Spatial Localization Across Kidney Compartments and Cell Types
sec.p: Using sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics from Engesser et al.18 (Figure 1a, Supplementary Methods), patient-level pseudobulk analyses confirmed increased classical and alternative complement pathway-related expression scores in AAV-GN kidneys compared with controls, consistent with the bulk NanoString findings (Figure 4a). Spatial compartment annotation showed that these signals were not confined to overtly inflamed regions. Both cCP_path and cAP_path were increased across inflamed glomerular and tubulointerstitial compartments, but also in noninflamed glomerular, tubulointerstitial, and tubular compartments, particularly for cAP_path (Figure 4b–c). Individual complement gene-expression patterns across compartments are shown in Supplementary Figure S5.

sec.p: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics from Sultana et al.19 further refined the cellular distribution of complement-related expression (Figure 1a, Supplementary Methods). At the patient level, AAV-GN kidneys showed increased cCP_path and C3 expression compared with controls (cAP_path could not be calculated because C3 was the only available gene from the predefined alternative pathway gene set in this data set; Figure 4d). Cell-type–resolved analyses showed that cCP_path expression was increased predominantly across immune cell populations, whereas C3 expression was increased across both immune and nonimmune kidney cell populations (Figure 4e–f). Among immune cells, the strongest signals involved myeloid-lineage populations, including macrophages, monocyte-derived cells, and neutrophils. Among nonimmune cells, C3 expression was particularly increased in parietal epithelial cells and tubular cells. Detailed cell-type–specific expression patterns for individual complement genes are shown in Supplementary Figures S6 and S7. In AAV-GN kidneys, CFH expression was predominantly observed in nonimmune kidney cell populations, whereas C5AR1 expression was broadly distributed across immune cell types, particularly myeloid-lineage populations, with detectable expression in selected nonimmune cell populations (Supplementary Figure S7).

sec.title: Cross-platform Reproducibility of Complement-Related Expression Signatures
sec.p: To quantitatively assess the robustness of intrarenal complement-related expression we performed a cross-cohort random-effects meta-analysis of standardized effect sizes (Cohen d) comparing AAV-GN and control kidneys across the 3 independent transcriptomic data sets (Supplementary Methods). Detailed results are provided in Supplementary Table S3 and summarized in Figure 5.

sec.p: Several complement genes showed large and consistent effect sizes across platforms. C1QB, C1QC, C3, CFB, and CFH showed strong concordance (random-effects d ≈ 1.8–2.3; I2 = 0%; all q < 10-8), and both classical (cCP_path) and alternative (cAP_path) pathway-related expression scores were similarly elevated (d ≈ 1.9; I2 = 0%), supporting reproducible increased expression of both complement pathway-related signatures in AAV-GN. Among membrane-bound regulators, CD46 was consistently decreased (d = −0.62; q = 3 × 10-3).

In contrast, C5 showed marked cross-platform heterogeneity (I2 = 96%, τ2 = 4.4) with a nonsignificant pooled effect estimate, whereas C5AR1, C1QA, and CFD also showed substantial between-study variability (I2 > 85%). Given the limited number of contributing data sets per gene (k = 2–3), heterogeneity estimates should be interpreted cautiously.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this multimodal study integrating circulating biomarkers, renal histopathology, and bulk and spatial transcriptomics in AAV-GN, we describe a layered and partially dissociated landscape of complement-related expression. AAV-GN kidneys exhibited a robust intrarenal complement-related transcriptional program involving proximal alternative pathway genes and classical pathway components, reproducibly increased across independent bulk and spatial transcriptomic data sets. This program was only weakly captured by circulating C3/C4 levels or routine glomerular immunofluorescence and was associated with kidney severity and long-term kidney and patient survival. Spatial transcriptomic data suggested contributions from both infiltrating immune cells and resident kidney compartments.

sec.title: Complement Assessment in AAV-GN is Multimodal and Partially Dissociated
sec.p: Overt hypocomplementemia was uncommon, consistent with previous reports and with the historical perception of AAV-GN as a pauci-immune disease.1,8,21 However, low or low-normal serum C3, but not C4, was associated with more severe kidney involvement and poorer prognosis, in line with multiple independent cohorts.5,6,22, 23, 24, 25, 26 At the tissue level, glomerular C3 deposition was observed in nearly half of biopsies, reinforcing that complement deposition is not exceptional in AAV-GN despite its pauci-immune classification.3,7,9,27,28 C1q deposition was less frequent,9,29 but identified patients with more severe renal disease and worse outcomes, consistent with the presence of classical pathway–related transcripts in the kidney and with previous reports suggesting classical or lectin pathway involvement in selected patients.30, 31, 32

Importantly, correlations between circulating complement levels, glomerular complement deposition, and intrarenal complement-related gene expression were weak across modalities. These findings indicate that serum levels, routine immunofluorescence, and transcriptomic readouts capture partially distinct dimensions of complement biology in AAV-GN. Intrarenal complement-related transcripts may arise from local production by resident kidney cells, infiltrating immune cells, regulatory feedback responses, or tissue remodeling, rather than reflecting a single linear continuum from systemic consumption to tissue deposition and local gene expression.

This layered interpretation is illustrated by CFH, one of the most consistently increased transcripts across data sets. CFH encodes factor H, a major negative regulator of the alternative pathway; its upregulation may therefore reflect a local regulatory or compensatory response rather than simply stronger complement effector signaling. Similar involvement of the factor H regulatory axis has been reported in other complement-associated glomerular diseases.33,34 Moreover, local CFH transcription does not necessarily imply effective protein-level regulation, because circulating factor H is largely hepatic in origin and its biological effect depends on protein abundance, localization, surface binding, and interactions with factor H–related proteins.35 Thus, whether intrarenal CFH expression reflects effective regulation, insufficient compensation, or both cannot be resolved from transcriptomic data alone.

sec.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Suggest Multicellular Sources of Complement-Related Expression
sec.p: Bulk complement pathway-related expression scores were strongly correlated with NanoString-derived immune cell signatures, especially macrophage, neutrophil, dendritic cell, and global leukocyte scores. This indicates that bulk complement-related expression is tightly coupled to the inflammatory cellular architecture of AAV-GN lesions, which is biologically expected given the central role of myeloid populations in ANCA-mediated kidney injury. However, this also highlights a key limitation of bulk transcriptomics—pathway-level expression scores cannot determine whether transcripts originate from infiltrating immune cells, resident kidney cells, or both.

Spatial transcriptomic analyses partially addressed this limitation. At the compartment level, classical and alternative pathway-related expression scores were increased not only in inflamed glomerular and tubulointerstitial regions, but also in noninflamed compartments, particularly for the alternative pathway score. At the cellular level, complement-related transcripts were detected across multiple immune and nonimmune kidney cell populations, with classical pathway expression being more prominent in immune cell populations, whereas C3 expression was observed across both immune and resident kidney compartments, including parietal epithelial and tubular cells. These data suggest a multicellular intrarenal complement-related transcriptional response, rather than a signal exclusively driven by infiltrating leukocytes. They do not, however, prove local complement protein activation or functional pathway activity at the cellular level.

The cross-platform meta-analysis further supported the reproducibility of this transcriptional signature. C1QB, C1QC, C3, CFB, CFH, and the predefined classical and alternative pathway-related scores showed consistent effect sizes across independent data sets. Conversely, heterogeneity for selected transcripts, including C5, C5AR1, C1QA, and CFD, emphasizes that some complement-related signals may vary according to tissue sampling, cellular composition, platform design, spatial resolution, or analytical pipelines, warranting dedicated prospective study.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study has several limitations. Its retrospective design resulted in incomplete availability of complement modalities for some patients, reflecting routine-care measurement of serum complement levels and the availability of residual diagnostic biopsy material for transcriptomic analyses. Although modality-specific subsets were broadly comparable to the overall cohort, residual selection bias cannot be excluded. Importantly, transcript abundance does not establish biochemical complement activation, and our findings should be interpreted as a descriptive characterization of complement-related transcriptional programs rather than as a direct readout of pathway activity. Indeed, we did not perform functional assays or measure circulating or urinary complement fragments (Ba/Bb, C3a, C5a, or soluble C5b-9). These assays require stringent preanalytical conditions and were not considered reliable for retrospective measurement in archived heterogeneous samples. Lastly, we also did not perform competing-risk regression or multiplicity correction across all survival contrasts; therefore, outcome analyses should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

sec.title: Translational Implications and Future Directions
sec.p: Despite these caveats, the reproducibility of intrarenal complement-related expression across independent transcriptomic platforms and its association with clinical outcomes, support the relevance of tissue-level complement profiling alongside circulating biomarkers and routine immunofluorescence in AAV-GN. Given the expanding therapeutic landscape of complement modulation in nephrology,36 our findings highlight the potential value of intrarenal profiling to refine biological stratification and generate hypotheses for therapeutic prioritization. In particular, the consistent upregulation of proximal alternative pathway genes, classical pathway components, and regulatory transcripts such as CFH, suggests that future biomarker and trial designs should look beyond terminal complement readouts and also consider upstream components37, 38, 39, 40 and regulators.41 This may be relevant in light of emerging evidence implicating local C3–C3aR signaling in injured tubular cells as a driver of persistent inflammation and tubulointerstitial fibrosis.42
Prospective studies will be needed to determine whether complement-based stratification can inform trial enrichment or therapeutic decisions and ultimately improve outcomes in AAV-GN.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: All data supporting the findings of this study are available within the paper and its Supplementary Information. NanoString nSolver data was deposited into the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under the accession number GSE298999. The clinical data is not publicly available owing to restrictions (information that could compromise the privacy of research participants) but is available from the corresponding author, BB, upon reasonable request.
The sequencing- and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics data sets are publicly available in GEO database under accession numbers GSE25013818 and GSE294965,19 respectively.
